title: Jeremiah 23:16–22
context: The LORD of Armies warns the people not to listen to prophets who speak visions of their own heart and promise peace to the stubborn (23:16–17). True prophets stand in the LORD’s council and turn people from evil (23:18, 22); these prophets ran without being sent (23:21). The storm of 23:19–20 reappears, with differences in wording, in 30:23–24.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says, “Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They teach you vanity. They speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says, “Don’t listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you.” Arminian readers see the people called to discern true from false prophecy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a command to test prophetic claims. The false prophets speak “a vision of their own heart,” and readers in this tradition see the source of a message as the decisive test.

verses.text: They say continually to those who despise me, ‘The LORD has said, “You will have peace;” ’ and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart they say, ‘No evil will come on you.’
verses.arminianNotes: “They say continually to those who despise me, ‘The LORD has said, “You will have peace.”’” Arminian readers see false assurance offered to the unrepentant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the danger of promising peace without repentance. Readers in this tradition commonly apply this to any preaching that comforts the stubborn while ignoring the call to turn.

verses.text: For who has stood in the council of the LORD, that he should perceive and hear his word? Who has listened to my word, and heard it?
verses.arminianNotes: “For who has stood in the council of the LORD, that he should perceive and hear his word?” Arminian readers see the true prophet as one who has heard God, unlike those who invent messages.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the council of the LORD as the source of authentic prophecy. Readers in this tradition compare scenes such as 1 Kings 22:19, cited by reference, where a prophet sees the heavenly council.

verses.text: Behold, the LORD’s storm, his wrath, has gone out. Yes, a whirling storm! It will burst on the head of the wicked.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, the LORD’s storm, his wrath, has gone out.” Arminian readers see the coming judgment the false prophets denied, pictured as a whirling storm on the wicked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment as certain. Jeremiah 30:23–24 repeats much of 23:19–20 in a new setting, and readers in this tradition note the reuse without harmonizing the differences in wording.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger will not return until he has executed and performed the intents of his heart. In the latter days, you will understand it perfectly.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD’s anger will not return until he has executed and performed the intents of his heart.” Arminian readers see God’s purposes in judgment carried through, with understanding coming later.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s purpose accomplished. “In the latter days, you will understand it perfectly” suggests that the meaning of these events becomes clear only afterward.

verses.text: I didn’t send these prophets, yet they ran. I didn’t speak to them, yet they prophesied.
verses.arminianNotes: “I didn’t send these prophets, yet they ran. I didn’t speak to them, yet they prophesied.” Arminian readers see self-appointed prophets acting without God’s commission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the absence of a divine call as the mark of false prophecy. Readers in this tradition connect this with Deuteronomy 18:20–22, cited by reference, on prophets who speak without being sent.

verses.text: But if they had stood in my council, then they would have caused my people to hear my words, and would have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their doings.
verses.arminianNotes: “But if they had stood in my council, then they would have caused my people to hear my words, and would have turned them from their evil way.” Arminian readers see true prophecy aimed at repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fruit of authentic prophecy in turning people from evil. Readers in both traditions commonly take this as a measure for preaching: faithful proclamation calls people to turn.
